**+1** — Reproduced on OpenCode v1.2.27 (Linux, 30GB RAM system).

**Working directory:** `~` (home directory, not a specific project)
**bash-language-server process:** Grew to **22.5 GB RSS + 5.6 GB swap** within ~8 minutes of starting OpenCode. CPU usage was 563% (26 threads), OOM score hit 984/1000.

```
PID 402991 — bash-language-server
VmRSS:  23,481,740 kB (22.4 GB)
VmSwap:  5,781,456 kB (5.5 GB)
VmSize: 105,270,736 kB (100 GB virtual)
Threads: 26
```

The system had only 293 MB free memory remaining (out of 30 GB) before I manually killed the process.

**Root cause confirmation:** OpenCode's LSP auto-launched bash-language-server against `$HOME`, which recursively scanned `node_modules/`, `.cache/`, `.local/`, etc. — triggering the `--external-sources` exponential expansion described in this issue.

**Workaround applied:** `kill <pid>` + adding `external-sources=false` to `~/.shellcheckrc`. Looking forward to the `OPENCODE_DISABLE_LSP` env var from PR #16271.

Closing as duplicate of #14304. The active fix appears to be in #15598, and I added a concrete repro note there showing this also affects package-name plugin installs once they resolve to node_modules file URLs.

**Workaround that works for me:**
Hide the session scrollbar via tui.json keybind. No scrollbar thumb = no hover-drag trigger.
Add this to  `~/.config/opencode/tui.json`:
```
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/tui.json",
  "keybinds": {
    "scrollbar_toggle": "f6"
  }
}

```
Then press F6 once after launching OpenCode in the IntelliJ terminal to hide the scrollbar.

Why it works: The bug is triggered by the scrollbar thumb reacting to mouse hover/move as if a drag is active. Hiding the scrollbar removes the thumb entirely, so there is nothing to trigger.

Environment:
- OpenCode 1.2.27
- IntelliJ IDEA 2025.3.4
- macOS 15.7.4 (Apple Silicon)

I was also running into this, although I feel either I am missing something or @jdocker8 might be mis-understanding the workflow right now.

As I understand it, when the system compacts the context, it sends a prompt to the agent to basically summarize the existing context. There is a long-ish prompt for this, and there is also the "What did we do so far?" prompt, I'm not sure how these work togehter, but what I observed was that it created a single long summary of the work done and next steps.

It is my understanding that this summary **IS** the compaction. That summary becomes the only awareness the model has of the previous context. As such you would not want to remove that even if in general you ask the agent not to summarize. From what I can tell there is nothing else fancy about the compaction, it's just a summary that replaces the previous context.

However, the "What did we do so far" and "Continue if you have next steps, or stop and ask for clarification if you are unsure how to proceed" **are** very problematic for all the reasons that have been stated here already. For me the issue was mainly with subagents, where they would end up compacting right before they returned so you would get:
* Very detailed summary
* "Continue if you have next steps, or stop and ask for clarification if you are unsure how to proceed"
* A very brief summary (since the model knows it _just_ output a full summary)

And since the task framework only returns the final output to the main agent, the main agent would get that super brief summary with no real information.

So, for fun, I decided to try the nuclear option: I just cut those additional user prompts out entirely. I adjusted the compact prompt a bit to make sure the agent clearly states if it thinks it should continue or not (with respect to the initial task to avoid the issue @poetislata described). That way, the agent is left with a detailed summary message, and it can then make the decision to keep working if the initial task is not complete or stop and have the summary be its final output. No user prompt injection required.

I haven't done a ton of testing, but I've at least confirmed it works to fix the subagent issue I was having. Here's my fork in case anyone else wants to try it: https://github.com/Jyers/opencode

> The `agent.set` function in `opencode/packages/app/src/context/local.tsx` at L226 incorrectly prioritizes the new agent's default model over the existing session-specific model. The line `model: item.model ?? prev?.model,` means that if the `item` (the new agent) has a default model (`item.model` is defined), it will unconditionally overwrite the `prev?.model` (which holds the user's manual model selection for the current session) when `setSaved` is called. This leads to manual selections being lost upon agent switches.
> 
> Location:opencode/packages/app/src/context/local.tsx
> 
> Modify the `agent.set` function in `opencode/packages/app/src/context/local.tsx` at line 226. Change the expression for the `model` property within the `next` state object from `item.model ?? prev?.model` to `prev?.model ?? item.model`. This simple change reverses the priority, ensuring that any existing session-specific model (which would include a user's manual selection) is preserved when an agent is switched. The new agent's default model (`item.model`) will only be applied if no model was previously set for the current session (`prev?.model` is undefined).
> 
> The original code `model: item.model ?? prev?.model` within the `agent.set` function meant that if the newly selected agent (`item`) had a default model (`item.model` was not `undefined`), that default would always be selected. This unconditionally overwrote any previous model in `prev?.model` that was manually set by the user for the current session. The fix `model: prev?.model ?? item.model` reverses this priority. It now instructs the system to first check if there's already a model set in the current session's state (`prev?.model`). If a model exists there, it will be used, thereby preserving the user's manual selection. If `prev?.model` is `undefined` (meaning no model has been explicitly set for the session yet), it will then fall back to using the new agent's default model (`item.model`). This ensures that user's explicit model choices are respected and not overwritten when merely switching agents, while still providing a sensible default if no specific model has been chosen for a session.
